etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English don, from Old English dōn, from Proto-West Germanic *dōn, from Proto-Germanic *dōną, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁- (“to put, place, do, make”).

For senses 4 and 5, compare Old Norse duga, whence Danish du.

The past tense form is from Middle English didde, dude, from Old English dyde, *diede, an unexpected development from Proto-Germanic *dedǭ/*dedē (the expected reflex would be *ded), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰédʰeh₁ti, an athematic e-reduplicated verb of the same root *dʰeh₁-.

The meaningless use of do in interrogative, negative, and affirmative sentences (e.g. "Do you like painting?" "Yes, I do"), existing in some form in most Germanic languages, is thought by some linguists to be one of the Brittonicisms in English, calqued from Brythonic. It is first recorded in Middle English, where it may have marked the perfective aspect, though in some cases the meaning seems to be imperfective. In Early Modern English, any meaning in such contexts was lost, making it a dummy auxiliary, and soon thereafter its use became mandatory in most questions and negations.

Doublets include deed, deem, and -dom, but not deal.

Other cognates include, via Latin, English feast, festival, fair (“celebration”), via Greek, English theo-, theme, thesis, and Sanskrit दधाति (dadhāti, “to put”), धातृ (dhātṛ, “creator”) and धातु (dhātu, “layer, element, root”).

definitions.definition: (auxiliary) A syntactic marker in a question whose main verb is not another auxiliary verb or be.
(auxiliary) A syntactic marker in negations with the indicative and imperative moods.

quote.citation: 1897 December (indicated as 1898), Winston Churchill, chapter IV, in The Celebrity: An Episode, New York, N.Y.: The Macmillan Company; London: Macmillan & Co., Ltd., →OCLC, page 51:
quote.text: “Well,” I answered, at first with uncertainty, then with inspiration, “he would do splendidly to lead your cotillon, if you think of having one.” ¶ “So you do not dance, Mr. Crocker?” ¶ I was somewhat set back by her perspicuity.

definitions.definition: (auxiliary) A syntactic marker for emphasis with the indicative, imperative, and subjunctive moods.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter VII, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “I don't know how you and the ‘head,’ as you call him, will get on, but I do know that if you call my duds a ‘livery’ again there'll be trouble. It's bad enough to go around togged out like a life saver on a drill day, but I can stand that 'cause I'm paid for it.  […] ”

quote.citation: 1950, C. S. Lewis, The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe:
quote.text: "Do stop it," said Susan; "it won't make things any better having a row between you two. Let's go and find Lucy."

definitions.definition: (pro-verb) A syntactic marker that refers back to an earlier verb and allows the speaker to avoid repeating the verb; in most dialects, not used with auxiliaries such as be, though it can be in AAVE.

quote.citation: 1930, George Gershwin, Ira Gershwin, Embraceable You:
quote.text: Don't be a naughty baby,Come to papa, come to papa, do!My sweet embraceable you.

definitions.definition: (auxiliary, archaic, dialectal) Used to form the present progressive of verbs.

quote.citation: 1844, William Barnes, “Evenén in the Village”, in Poems of Rural Life in the Dorset Dialect:
quote.text: ...An' the dogs do bark, an' the rooks be a-vled to the elems high and dark, an' the water do roar at mill.

definitions.definition: (auxiliary) A syntactic marker.
(transitive) To perform; to execute.

quote.citation: 2013 June 21, Oliver Burkeman, “The tao of tech”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 2, page 48:
quote.text: The dirty secret of the internet is that all this distraction and interruption is immensely profitable. Web companies like to boast about […], or offering services that let you "stay up to date with what your friends are doing", […] and so on. But the real way to build a successful online business is to be better than your rivals at undermining people's control of their own attention.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To cause, make (someone) (do something).

definitions.definition: (intransitive, transitive) To suffice.

quote.text: "Here," she said, "take your old Bunny! He'll do to sleep with you!" And she dragged the Rabbit out by one ear, and put him into the Boy's arms.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be reasonable or acceptable.
(ditransitive) To have (as an effect).
(especially England, intransitive) To fare well; to thrive; to prosper; (of livestock) to fatten.

quote.citation: 1908 September 21, “The fattening beast”, in Mark Lane Express Agricultural Journal‎[4], page 340:
quote.text: A big framed beast takes a lot of food — expensive food at that [—] to keep it doing  […]

quote.text: That farm would go like a rick a-fire. It would do: it would go forward and prosper and make him his money.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To fare, perform (well or poorly).

quote.text: Plastics are energy-rich substances, which is why many of them burn so readily. Any organism that could unlock and use that energy would do well in the Anthropocene. Terrestrial bacteria and fungi which can manage this trick are already familiar to experts in the field.

definitions.definition: (transitive, chiefly in questions) To have as one's job.
(transitive) To perform the tasks or actions associated with (something).
(transitive) To cook.

quote.text: We went down below, and the galley-slave did some ham and eggs, and the first lieutenant, who was aged 19, told me about Sicily, and time went like a flash.

quote.text: No tourist can get credit for seeing America first without doing New York, the Wonderful Town, the Baghdad-on-Hudson, the dream in the eye of the Kansas hooker  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To treat in a certain way.

quote.citation: 2018, Kate Atkinson, Transcription, →ISBN, page 291:

(transitive) To impersonate or depict.
(transitive, with 'a' and the name of a person, place, event, etc.) To copy or emulate the actions or behaviour that is associated with the person or thing mentioned.
(transitive, slang) To kill.

quote.text: About a year ago, a boy name Brandon got got here in Baltimore. Stuck and burned before he passed.  […]  Wasn't no need for y'all to do him the way y'all did.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang) To deal with for good and all; to finish up; to undo; to ruin; to do for.

quote.citation: 1870, Charles Reade, Put Yourself in His Place:
quote.text: Sometimes they lie in wait in these dark streets, and fracture his skull,  […]  or break his arm, or cut the sinew of his wrist; and that they call doing him.

definitions.definition: (transitive, informal) To punish for a misdemeanor.
(transitive, slang) To have sex with. (See also do it)

quote.text: Deme. Villaine what haſt thou done?A. That which thou canſt not vndoe.Chiron. Thou haſt vndone our mother.Aron. Villaine I haue done thy mother.

quote.citation: 2008, Donna Hill, On the Line‎[13], page 84:
quote.text: The uninhibited woman within wanted to do him right there on the countertop, but I remained composed.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cheat or swindle.

quote.citation: 1852, Thomas De Quincey, Sir William Hamilton:
quote.text: He was not to be done, at his time of life, by frivolous offers of a compromise that might have secured him seventy-five per cent.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To convert into a certain form; especially, to translate.
(transitive, intransitive) To finish.
(stock exchange) To cash or to advance money for, as a bill or note.
(informal, transitive, ditransitive) To make or provide.
(informal, transitive) To injure (one's own body part).

definitions.definition: (obsolete, UK, slang) A cheat; a swindler.
(obsolete, UK, slang) An act of swindling; a fraud or deception.
(UK, slang) A homicide.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Coined by Italian musicologist Giovanni Battista Doni in 1635 as an easier-to-sing open-syllable revision to the solmization ut of Guido of Arezzo, from the first syllable of Latin Dominus (“The Lᴏʀᴅ”) (speculated by some to be an ulterior abbreviation of Giovanni Battista Doni) on the pattern of other Latinate solfège with the stated justification that God is the tonic and root of the world.

definitions.definition: (music) A syllable used in solfège to represent the first and eighth tonic of a major scale.
(archaic) Abbreviation of ditto.[3]
